# Local code search MCP for Claude Code that uses fewer tokens than grep

**TL;DR** — Yes: xerj is a local code search MCP for Claude Code that uses fewer tokens than grep. It indexes the repository once, then `xerj search` and `xerj def` return ranked passages with path:line. On psf/requests, measured 2026-10-19, one answer was 1,303 bytes against 25,150 bytes of `rg` output.

## Agent prompt

```text
Read https://xerj.org/llms.txt. Install xerj, start a node with xerj --insecure --data-dir ~/xerj-data, run xerj autoindex on this repository, run xerj init so the xerj MCP server is registered, then answer my next code question with one xerj search or xerj def call and cite path:line instead of opening whole files.
```

## Commands

### Command 1

Note: Install the release binary into ~/.local/bin (the installer checks its SHA-256).

```sh
curl -fsSL https://xerj.org/get | sh
```

### Command 2

Note: Start a single-user node on localhost:9200 in its own terminal.

```sh
xerj --insecure --data-dir ./xerj-data
```

### Command 3

Note: Index the repository once; code files get defs and symbols with line numbers.

```sh
xerj autoindex ./requests --prefix req
```

### Command 4

Note: Three ranked passages with path:line, each body capped at 400 characters.

```sh
xerj search --prefix req -k 3 --full 400 "rebuild auth on redirect strip authorization"
```

### Command 5

Note: Exact definition lookup: the declaration line and the file's symbol list.

```sh
xerj def --prefix req should_strip_auth
```

### Command 6

Note: Register xerj mcp in .mcp.json for Claude Code (and Cursor or Codex when present).

```sh
xerj init
```

## Run it

The installer puts one binary in `~/.local/bin`. Start a node in its own terminal, index the repository once, and then ask. These are the exact commands and output from a scratch HOME with v1.0.0-rc.97 and psf/requests at commit 611c6162.

```sh
curl -fsSL https://xerj.org/get | sh
xerj --insecure --data-dir ./xerj-data &
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/psf/requests
xerj autoindex ./requests --prefix req
```

```text
done in 2.9s — 1 dataset, 1571 records live, 0 duplicate aliases, 0 junk records, 1 junk/skipped file (543.9 docs/sec)
xerj-done ok=true exit=3 reason=completed-with-junk wall=3.0s files=95 records=1571 datasets=1 junk_files=1 code_files=36 code_files_indexed=36 code_files_junked=0
```

Exit 3 means the run completed and skipped one file it could not use; all 36 code files were indexed.

Ask with the words the code uses. The answer names the function, the file and the line.

```sh
xerj search --prefix req -k 3 --full 400 "rebuild auth on redirect strip authorization"
```


When you know the symbol, `xerj def` is shorter still.

```sh
xerj def --prefix req should_strip_auth
```

```text

```

## Give it to Claude Code over MCP

Run `xerj init` in the project. It writes `.mcp.json` for Claude Code and keeps the MCP entries already there. Cursor and Codex get the same entry when their config folders exist. Keep the node running, because `xerj mcp` does not start one.

```json
{"mcpServers": {"xerj": {"command": "xerj", "args": ["mcp", "--url", "http://localhost:9200"]}}}
```

## Measured on 2026-10-19

One question, three ways to answer it, on the same checkout (95 files indexed, 36 of them code). Bytes are what lands in the agent's context.

| Method | Output | Bytes | Wall time, 5 runs |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `rg -n -i redirect` | 282 lines from 17 files | 25,150 | 5 to 7 ms |
| Open the 17 matching files | whole files | 447,383 | n/a |
| `xerj search -k 3 --full 400` | 3 passages, `sessions.py:309` first | 1,303 | 8 to 23 ms |
| `xerj def should_strip_auth` | declaration plus symbol list | 949 | not timed |

The ratio is 19 times fewer bytes for the search, measured once on one repository. ripgrep is faster per call. A byte is not a token, so treat this as a size comparison, not a token count. The published agent benchmark is the token number: 9,982 output tokens for xerj against 26,477 for the baseline agent, 2.7 times fewer, over 8 tasks.

## How it compares

| Tool | Runs locally | Ranked results | file:line | MCP server | Setup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| xerj | yes | yes, BM25 | yes | yes, 23 tools | install, start node, index once |
| ripgrep | yes | no, every match | yes | no | none |
| Zoekt | yes | yes | yes | no | index server |
| GitHub code search | no | yes | yes | no | repo on GitHub, API limits |
| Vector database plus embedder | depends | yes, semantic | only if you store it | depends | embedder, chunker, store |

## When not to use xerj

- You need regular expressions over source. xerj has no regex search; use ripgrep.
- The repository is small enough to read whole, or you only search it once. The index costs a node and a step.
- You need natural-language matching with no shared words. The default ranking is lexical. The default embedder is lexical feature hashing; `--embed-mode neural` downloads all-MiniLM-L6-v2, about 90 MB, and is opt-in.
- The machine must stay idle. The published 15-repository run measured 8% CPU and 8.3 GB for an idle xerj node against 0.03% and 119 MB for Zoekt.

## FAQ

### Is there a local code search MCP for Claude Code that uses fewer tokens than grep?

Yes. xerj runs on your machine, indexes the repository once and serves the index through `xerj mcp`. On psf/requests a ranked answer was 1,303 bytes where `rg -n -i redirect` printed 25,150 bytes.

### MCP server grep alternative with fewer tokens: which tools does xerj expose?

On main `xerj mcp` serves 23 tools, or 20 in a build with no hub key, including `xerj_search`, `xerj_code_search`, `xerj_map` and the three hub tools. Run `xerj init` in the project to register it.

### Is xerj faster than ripgrep?

Not per call. Two sessions of five runs on psf/requests took 8 to 23 ms for `xerj search` and 5 to 7 ms for `rg`. The saving is in what the agent reads afterwards, not in wall time.

### Does it understand code or only words?

Code files are parsed with tree-sitter, so `xerj def` finds a declaration by name. Ranking is lexical BM25 by default; `xerj search` says so on its first line.

### What happens when my wording does not match the code?

Lexical ranking can miss. Our first phrasing, about stripping the Authorization header when a redirect changes host, ranked tests and `rebuild_method` above `rebuild_auth`. Rephrasing with the words in the code fixed it.

### How much does this save in a full agent session?

The published coding-agent benchmark measured 2.7 times fewer output tokens than the baseline agent over 8 tasks and 16 runs per arm. Your repository and agent will give a different number.
